name: Linux Command Line
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Move around the filesystem, manage files and permissions, and combine commands with pipes.

lesson.intro: The shell lets you control a computer by typing commands, and small commands combine into powerful ones. This lesson covers moving around the filesystem, managing files, permissions, pipes and redirection, searching with grep and find, and managing processes and environment variables.

sections.title: Navigating and managing files
sections.body:
Linux arranges everything in one tree that starts at `/`, the root. Your home directory is usually `/home/<name>`, and `~` is short for it. The shell always has a current directory, and `pwd` prints it.

- An absolute path starts with `/` and means the same thing from anywhere: `/etc/hosts`.
- A relative path starts from the current directory: `docs/notes.txt`.
- `.` is the current directory and `..` is its parent. `cd -` jumps back to the directory you were in before.

`ls` lists a directory. `ls -l` adds permissions, owner, size and date, and `ls -a` also shows hidden files, whose names start with a dot, such as `.bashrc`.

To manage files: `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates a directory and any missing parents, `cp` copies (add `-r` for a directory), `mv` moves or renames, and `rm` deletes (add `-r` for a directory). There is no trash can, so `rm` is permanent.
sections.code:
pwd                       # /home/ana
cd projects/site          # relative path
cd ..                     # up one level: /home/ana/projects
cd /var/log               # absolute path
cd -                      # back to /home/ana/projects
mkdir -p backup/2024/june
cp -r site backup/2024/june/
mv draft.txt final.txt    # rename
sections.tip: Press Tab to complete file and directory names. It saves typing and catches typos before they happen.

check.question: Which command takes you back to the directory you were in just before the last `cd`?
choices: cd ..
cd -
cd ~
cd /
check.explanation: cd - switches to the previous directory. cd .. goes to the parent, cd ~ goes home, and cd / goes to the root.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.body:
Every file has an owner, a group, and three sets of permissions: for the owner (user), for the group, and for everyone else (others). `ls -l` shows them as ten characters, such as `-rwxr-xr--`.

The first character is the type: `-` for a file, `d` for a directory. Then come three groups of `rwx` for user, group and others. `r` is read, `w` is write, `x` is execute, and `-` means that permission is missing.

On a directory, `r` lets you list its contents and `x` lets you enter it with `cd` and reach the files inside.

`chmod` changes permissions in two styles. Symbolic: `chmod u+x script.sh` adds execute for the owner, and `chmod go-w file` removes write from group and others. Octal: each of the three groups is one digit, the sum of r=4, w=2 and x=1. So 7 is rwx, 6 is rw-, 5 is r-x and 4 is r--, and `chmod 754 file` gives `rwxr-xr--`.
sections.code:
ls -l deploy.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 ana staff 210 Jun 3 10:12 deploy.sh
./deploy.sh               # Permission denied: no x bit
chmod u+x deploy.sh
ls -l deploy.sh
-rwxr--r-- 1 ana staff 210 Jun 3 10:12 deploy.sh
chmod 640 notes.txt       # rw- r-- ---
sections.tip: `chmod 777` lets everyone change the file. It is almost never the right fix for a permission error.

check.question: Which octal mode gives the owner read and write access and gives nobody else any access?
check.explanation: Read plus write is 4 + 2 = 6 for the owner, and 0 for group and others. 644 lets everyone read, 700 adds execute, and 400 is read-only.

sections.title: Pipes and redirection
sections.body:
Every command has three standard streams: standard input (stdin, number 0), standard output (stdout, 1) and standard error (stderr, 2). By default, output and errors both go to the terminal.

- `cmd > file` sends stdout to a file, replacing what was in it.
- `cmd >> file` appends to the file instead.
- `cmd 2> file` sends stderr to a file.
- `cmd > file 2>&1` sends both to the same file. Redirections are applied left to right, so point stdout at the file first, then point stderr at stdout.
- `cmd < file` reads stdin from a file.

`/dev/null` is a special file that discards anything written to it, so `2> /dev/null` hides error messages.

A pipe `|` connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin, so small tools combine into bigger ones. `sort` sorts lines, `uniq` removes adjacent duplicates (`-c` counts them), `wc -l` counts lines, and `head -n 3` keeps the first three.
sections.code:
ls -l /etc > listing.txt             # overwrite listing.txt
date >> log.txt                      # append a line
find / -name "*.conf" 2> /dev/null   # hide permission errors
sort names.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
sections.tip: `uniq` only removes duplicates that sit next to each other, so sort first.

check.question: Which stream does a pipe `|` pass to the next command?
choices: Standard output only
Standard error only
Both standard output and standard error
Standard input of the first command
check.explanation: A pipe carries stdout. Error messages still go to the terminal unless you redirect them, for example with 2>&1 before the pipe.

sections.title: Searching with grep and find
sections.body:
`grep` prints the lines that match a pattern. It reads the files you name, or stdin when used in a pipe.

- `grep error app.log` prints lines containing "error".
- `-i` ignores case, `-n` shows line numbers, `-v` shows lines that do not match, and `-c` counts matching lines.
- `-r` searches every file under a directory.

`find` walks a directory tree and prints the paths that pass its tests:

- `find . -name "*.txt"` matches names below the current directory.
- `find . -type d -name node_modules` matches directories only (`-type f` is regular files).
- `find /var/log -size +10M` matches files bigger than 10 MB, and `-mtime -1` matches files changed in the last day.

Quote patterns like `"*.txt"`. Without quotes, the shell expands `*.txt` using the files in the current directory before `find` even starts, so find receives the wrong arguments.
sections.code:
grep -n "TODO" src/app.js
grep -ri "timeout" config/
ps aux | grep nginx
find . -name "*.log" -mtime -1
find ~ -type f -size +100M
sections.tip: grep searches inside files; find searches for files by name, type, size or age.

check.question: Which command prints every line of app.log that does NOT contain DEBUG?
choices: grep -n DEBUG app.log
grep -c DEBUG app.log
grep -v DEBUG app.log
find app.log -not DEBUG
check.explanation: -v inverts the match, printing only lines without the pattern. -n adds line numbers to matches and -c counts them.

sections.title: Processes, environment variables and PATH
sections.body:
A running program is a process, and each one has a process ID (PID). `ps aux` lists every process; `top` shows them live.

`kill PID` sends a signal. By default it is SIGTERM (15), which asks the process to stop and lets it clean up first. `kill -9 PID` sends SIGKILL, which ends the process immediately with no cleanup, so use it only when SIGTERM does not work. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the program in the foreground.

Jobs are processes started from your current shell:
- `command &` starts it in the background.
- Ctrl+Z pauses (stops) the foreground job.
- `jobs` lists them, `bg %1` resumes job 1 in the background, and `fg %1` brings it to the foreground.

Environment variables are named values that programs read, such as `HOME` and `USER`. `NAME=value` sets a variable in the current shell only; `export NAME` passes it on to every program you start from that shell.

`PATH` is a colon-separated list of directories. When you type a command name, the shell searches them in order and runs the first match. `which name` shows which file that is.
sections.code:
sleep 300 &                        # [1] 4821
jobs                               # [1]+ Running   sleep 300 &
kill %1                            # same as: kill 4821
export API_URL="https://api.example.com"
echo $PATH                         # /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"      # add a directory to the front
which python3                      # the file that will run
sections.tip: Variables you export last only for the current shell session. Put the export line in `~/.bashrc` to keep it.

check.question: You run `sleep 500`, press Ctrl+Z, then run `bg`. What state is sleep in now?
choices: Stopped (paused)
Running in the background
Terminated
Running in the foreground
check.explanation: Ctrl+Z pauses the job and bg resumes it in the background, so it keeps running while you get your prompt back. fg would bring it to the foreground instead.

keyTerms.definition: A path that starts at the root /, so it means the same thing from any directory.
Permissions written as three digits for user, group and others, each the sum of r=4, w=2, x=1.
Stream 2, where programs write error messages; it is separate from standard output.
The | operator, which feeds one command's standard output into the next command's standard input.
The process ID, a number that identifies a running process.
A message sent to a process, such as SIGTERM (please stop) or SIGKILL (stop now).
A named value, such as HOME, that exported shells pass on to the programs they start.
The list of directories the shell searches, in order, to find the program for a command name.

summary: Absolute paths start at `/`; relative paths start where you are, and `..` means the parent directory.
Permissions are rwx for user, group and others; each octal digit adds r=4, w=2, x=1.
`>` overwrites, `>>` appends, `2>` redirects errors, and `|` feeds one command's output into the next.
grep finds lines inside files; find finds files by name, type, size or age.
`kill` sends SIGTERM by default, `export` passes variables to child programs, and PATH is searched left to right.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend what happens when they type `grep error app.log | wc -l` and press Enter: how the shell finds each program, what the pipe does, and what ends up on the screen.

questions.question: What does `mkdir -p reports/2024/q1` do when reports does not exist yet?
choices: Fails because the parent directory reports is missing
Creates one directory literally named reports/2024/q1
Creates reports, then 2024 inside it, then q1 inside that
Creates only q1, in the current directory
questions.explanation: -p creates every missing parent along the path and does not complain if some already exist. Without -p, mkdir fails with "No such file or directory".

questions.question: Type the command that lists the current directory including hidden files, whose names start with a dot.
questions.explanation: Plain ls skips names that start with a dot. -a shows them, including the . and .. entries; -A shows them without . and ..

questions.question: This was meant to copy the site directory into backup. Why did it fail?
questions.code:
cp site backup/
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'site'
choices: backup/ must be created with touch first
cp needs -r to copy a directory and its contents
cp cannot copy into a directory; mv is needed
The source directory needs a trailing slash
questions.explanation: cp copies single files unless you ask for a recursive copy. cp -r site backup/ copies the directory and its contents.

questions.question: You are in /var/www/html. What absolute path does `../../log/nginx` refer to?
choices: /var/www/log/nginx
/log/nginx
/var/www/html/log/nginx
/var/log/nginx
questions.explanation: The first .. goes up to /var/www, the second to /var, and then log/nginx is added: /var/log/nginx.

questions.question: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x---` for backup.sh. Who can run it?
choices: The owner and members of the file's group
Only the owner
Everyone on the system
Only members of the group, not the owner
questions.explanation: The user triplet rwx and the group triplet r-x both include x. The others triplet --- has nothing, so everyone else cannot run, read or change it.

questions.question: What octal number do you pass to chmod to set `rwxr-xr--`?
questions.explanation: rwx is 4+2+1 = 7, r-x is 4+1 = 5, and r-- is 4. Together: 754.

questions.question: Complete the command so the owner can execute deploy.sh, without changing anyone else's permissions.
choices: +x
u+x
u=x
questions.explanation: u+x adds execute for the owner only. +x adds it for everyone, 777 gives everyone full access, and u=x sets the owner to execute only, removing their read and write.

questions.question: A directory has mode `drw-r--r--`. Its owner, a normal user, tries to `cd` into it. What happens?
choices: It works, because r is enough to enter a directory
It fails: entering a directory needs the x permission
It works, because owners always have full access
It fails, because entering a directory needs the w bit
questions.explanation: On directories, x means "may enter and reach files inside". With rw- the owner has no x, so cd fails with Permission denied. Owners get no automatic bypass; only root does.

questions.question: missing.txt does not exist. What ends up in out.txt after `ls missing.txt 2>&1 > out.txt`?
choices: The error message, since 2>&1 sends it to the file
The error message twice, once per redirection
The literal text 2>&1 followed by the error
Nothing; the error still appears in the terminal
questions.explanation: Redirections run left to right. 2>&1 points stderr at wherever stdout points at that moment, the terminal. Then > moves only stdout to the file. Write ls missing.txt > out.txt 2>&1 to capture both.

questions.question: Complete the pipeline so it prints the most common line in names.txt together with its count.
choices: uniq -c
wc -l
uniq
grep -c
questions.explanation: After sorting, identical lines sit together, and uniq -c collapses each group into one line prefixed with its count. sort -rn then puts the biggest count first. Plain uniq would drop the counts.

questions.question: A script runs this line every hour. Complete it so each run adds the date to the end of log.txt instead of replacing the file.
questions.explanation: >> appends to the file. > would truncate it every hour, leaving only the latest date. | expects a command, not a file, and 2> redirects only errors.

questions.question: What does `grep -c error app.log` print?
choices: The total number of times error appears
Every line containing error, with line numbers
The number of lines that contain error
The names of the files that contain error
questions.explanation: -c counts matching lines, so a line with "error" twice still counts once. -n would print the lines with numbers, and -l would print file names.

questions.question: Type a find command that lists everything under the current directory whose name ends in `.py`.
questions.explanation: find starts at . (the current directory) and -name tests each file name against the pattern. The quotes stop the shell from expanding *.py before find sees it.

questions.question: This command fails when run in a directory that contains a.txt and b.txt. Why?
questions.code:
find docs -name *.txt
find: paths must precede expression: `b.txt'
choices: The shell expanded *.txt before find ran; quote it
find cannot search inside a directory named docs
-name only accepts exact file names, not patterns
find needs -type f before -name to work
questions.explanation: The shell replaced *.txt with a.txt b.txt, so find received "-name a.txt b.txt" and choked on the extra word. Writing -name "*.txt" passes the pattern through to find.

questions.question: What does `kill 4821` do?
choices: Sends SIGKILL, which ends the process instantly
Pauses the process until you resume it with fg
Deletes the program file that process 4821 runs
Sends SIGTERM, asking the process to exit cleanly
questions.explanation: With no signal given, kill sends SIGTERM (15), which a program can catch to save its work and exit. SIGKILL needs kill -9 and cannot be caught.

questions.question: After the first line, every command fails. What went wrong?
questions.code:
PATH=~/bin
ls
bash: ls: command not found
choices: ~/bin must be created with mkdir -p first
PATH must be written in lowercase as path
PATH was replaced, not extended; use PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
ls is built into the shell and cannot be found through PATH
questions.explanation: The assignment threw away /usr/bin and /bin, so the shell no longer finds ls. Prepending keeps the old list: PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH".

questions.question: You set `API_KEY=abc123` in your shell, but a script you run cannot see it. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.answer: A plain assignment creates a shell variable that only the current shell can see. Run `export API_KEY` (or `export API_KEY=abc123`) so programs started from the shell inherit it.
questions.explanation: Child processes receive only exported variables. You can also set a variable for one command: API_KEY=abc123 ./script.sh.
